subtype: Hearing constant shoulds from family [Receiver]
passage: Every Sunday lunch at the Lucknow flat, Rashmi Bua said it. "Deepak, you should do an MBA. You should settle by twenty-seven. My friend's son did both, and look at him now." She said it while heaping more kebabs on his plate. Deepak loved her. She had paid for his school trip when his father was ill. But every "should" landed like a small stone in his chest. He wanted to study product design, not an MBA, and marriage felt far away. This Sunday, when she started, he put down his fork. "Bua, I know you say this because you care about me. That means a lot." She smiled. "So?" "So I'm applying for design courses. I'd like you to see my portfolio. And I'll think about marriage when I'm ready." Rashmi Bua was quiet for a moment. Then she said, "Show me the portfolio after lunch."

qa.a: He wanted to study product design, not an MBA.

qa.a: Deepak feels love and gratitude toward her, but each should also lands like a small stone of pressure in his chest.

qa.a: He thanked her for caring, then stated his own choice clearly and invited her to see his portfolio, keeping both respect and independence.

qa.q: How might Rashmi Bua have felt when Deepak put down his fork?
qa.a: She might have felt surprised and a little unsure, then curious enough to want to see his portfolio.

He almost laughed. "You'll never let me say that."
"Maybe once," she said, and squeezed his hand.

For most of my first year, every phone call with Keerthana akka ended the same way. "You should switch to engineering. You should think about marriage early, like me. You should stop wasting time on history." She said it kindly. She had helped me with every exam since Class 5, and I looked up to her more than anyone. That was the problem. Her "shoulds" felt like love and like a weight at the same time.
I tried arguing. We fought. I tried agreeing. I felt hollow. Finally, one Sunday, I said, "Akka, I admire you so much. Your advice matters. But I love history, and I'm staying. Can you trust me on this one?" She was silent. Then she said, "Send me your essay. The one you got an A on." I did. She called back and said, "Okay. It's good."
It wasn't a full yes. But it was enough.
— Dhruv

passage: Salma ran the only computer training centre in Tarikere, and every night she wrote the same line in her notebook: "I should be more productive." Every night she felt guilty, because the line was never crossed off. There were fees to collect, a new course to design, a leaking roof to fix. One evening Ujjwal, who taught the typing class, saw the notebook. "Every day the same sentence?" She nodded, ashamed. "It makes me feel lazy before I even start." He picked up a pencil. "What if it said: 'I'd like to be more productive. Tomorrow's one step is...' " She thought. "...call the roofer." He wrote it down. The next morning she called the roofer before the first class. It took four minutes. That night she wrote, "I'd like to finish the course outline. One step: write the first two lessons." She did those too.

qa.q: What did Salma do the next morning before the first class?
qa.a: She called the roofer before the first class.

qa.a: It made her feel guilty and lazy every night, even before she started, because it was never crossed off.

qa.a: Turning the demand into a wish plus one concrete step made the task small and inviting, so the guilt dropped and she acted.

qa.a: Ujjwal would probably be pleased and encouraged that a small change in words made such a difference.

I'm dumb at reading." Their grandmother, knitting in the corner, said, "Stupid is a big word for a small thing. Which word stopped you?" Irawati pointed. "This one." "Then that's the one to practise. Not your whole head." Ajji wrote "though" and "through" on a slate, side by side. Irawati read them three times. Then she opened the book again, slowly, by the flickering lantern.

That's a thing you can practise." Trisha looked at the pile of tags. "Only the short ones," she said, and picked up a pen.

When he found out at 11:30, I expected the usual from new joiners: "I'm useless, I'm hopeless, I'll never get this." Instead he came to my desk and said, "I forgot the client meeting. Friday night
I forgot the meeting with Joseph today. He'd come all the way from Kochi to discuss the community library project, and I was at home fixing the gas stove. He waited at the café for forty minutes.
My first thought when I saw his messages was: I'm useless. A useless, careless person. I could feel myself sliding into that old place.
Then I stopped. Let me write this properly.
What I did: forgot a meeting I had agreed to.
What I feel: irresponsible and embarrassed. Joseph gave up his afternoon.
What I'll do: call him tomorrow morning, apologise without excuses, offer to travel to Kochi next time. Put every meeting in my phone with an alarm.
Written like that, it's a bad mistake. It isn't a bad person. I still have to fix it. But I can.
Yogesh
